findings.text: Within the first lines, a newcomer can say what Athena is and why it might matter: one model does the work, a second checks it, and every step's cost is recorded. This is the page's strongest part.
findings.source: Header lede: "Athena is an open-source system, written in Rust, that turns a short request into a change to a code repository. It shows how it read the request, has one AI model do the work and a different one check it, and records what each step cost."

findings.text: The next step is linked in the header, so the reader does not have to scroll through the whole study to find it. The Next steps section gives a repo link, an install command and a sample request.
findings.source: Header lede: "Next step: install Athena or read firstmate itself"

findings.text: On Athena's own site, almost all of the page is about a different project's internals. Athena's main job, turning a request into a change, appears only in one sentence and is never shown. A newcomer who came to learn about Athena may wonder why they are reading about firstmate's backlog.
findings.source: Title "Athena explains how firstmate handles work" and the sections States, Counters, Transitions

findings.text: The page states why the study exists, and the claim links to commit-pinned file lines back that up. This builds trust, but the reader has to work out alone that this is a sample of Athena's output.
findings.source: Header lede: "Athena made this study of firstmate to show that it can read an unfamiliar project and explain it with every statement traced to a claim, and every claim to lines in the project's own files."

findings.text: Start here is well ordered: key words are defined up front, then a numbered walk through one task. A reader can follow firstmate without reading the cards.
findings.source: Start here: "The three parts below say what firstmate is, follow one piece of work, and say what happens when something fails or has no limit."

findings.text: Opaque ids like t1–t11 and c1–c44 are used before a reader knows what they point to. The bare counter line tells a newcomer almost nothing.
findings.source: Counters: "places-held, changed by transitions t1, t3, t4, t9, t11"

findings.text: Some definitions are circular or weak: "wake" is never defined, and "ship" is described mostly by what is next to it. Other words such as "endpoint", "durable record" and "pin" in the secondmate sense appear without a plain explanation.
findings.source: Glossary: "stale wake — A wake after which the agent inspects a worker..."; "ship — A kind of task, named next to scouts."

findings.text: The ready→ready self-loop needs a long explanation, and repeated hedges like "The cited text states no..." make several passages slow to read for a first-time visitor.
findings.source: t10 card: "The task stays Ready because merging does not end it: it is Done only when teardown later returns the worktree..."

findings.text: The install step assumes the reader has already cloned the repo and gives no prerequisites, for example a Rust toolchain. A newcomer will need the linked repo to actually get started.
findings.source: Next steps: "Install Athena from a checkout of its repository: ./setup.sh"

findings.text: Being open about what was not run is good for trust. But this note describes Athena's internal process and means little to a newcomer without more context.
findings.source: Limits of this study, f3: "A first reading of the pinned tree missed these paths..."
